question.text: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z =y\ln x + x\ln y + 1$ at the point $(1,1,1).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

\[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (y\ln x + x\ln y + 1) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac yx + \ln y \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (y\ln x + x\ln y + 1) \\[5pt] &= \ln x + \dfrac xy \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (1,1) &= \dfrac 11 + \ln 1 = 1 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (1,1) &= \ln 1+\dfrac 11 = 1 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

\begin{align*} z - 1 &= (x-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,1) + (y-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,1) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= 1\cdot (x-1) + 1\cdot (y-1) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= x + y - 2 \\[5pt] -x -y + z + 1 &= 0 \\[5pt] x + y - z - 1 &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = x^3 y^2 - 2$ at the point $(1,2,2).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as \[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} ( x^3 y^2 - 2 ) \\[5pt] & = 3x^2y^2 \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} ( x^3 y^2 - 2 ) \\[5pt] & = 2x^3y \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (1,2)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (1,2) & = 3(1^2)(2^2) = 12 \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} (1,2) & = 2(1^3)(2) = 4 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane: \begin{align*} z - 2 &= (x - 1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,2) + (y - 2)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,2) \\[5pt] z - 2 &= 12(x - 1) + 4(y - 2) \\[5pt] z - 2 &= 12x + 4y - 20 \\[5pt] 12x + 4y - z - 18 & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Determine the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = 4x^2 + 9y^2 - 7$ at the point $(1,-1,6).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as \[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (4x^2 + 9y^2 - 7) \\[5pt] & = 8x \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} ( 4x^2 + 9y^2 - 7 ) \\[5pt] & = 18y \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (1, -1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (1,-1) & = 8(1) = 8 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (1,-1) & = 18(-1) = -18 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane: \begin{align*} z - 6 &= (x - 1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,-1) + (y - (-1))\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,-1) \\[5pt] z - 6 &= 8(x - 1) - 18(y+1) \\[5pt] z - 6 &= 8x - 18y - 26 \\[5pt] %-8x + 18y + z + 20 &= 0 \\[5pt] 8x - 18y - z - 20 &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Determine the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = x^2 - 2y^2 + 3$ at the point $(0,1,1).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as \[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (x^2 - 2y^2 + 3) \\[5pt] & = 2x \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} ( x^2 - 2y^2 + 3 ) \\[5pt] & = -4y \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (0,1) & = 2(0) = 0 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (0,1) & = -4(1) = -4 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane: \begin{align*} z - 1 &= (x - 0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,1) + (y - 1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,1) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= 0x - 4(y - 1) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= -4y + 4 \\[5pt] 4y + z - 5 & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = \sqrt{x^2+2y^3}-y$ at the point $(3,2,3).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

\[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\sqrt{x^2+2y^3}-y \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{2\sqrt{x^2+2y^3}} \cdot 2x - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {x}{\sqrt{x^2+2y^3}} \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left (\sqrt{x^2+2y^3}-y \right ) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{2\sqrt{x^2+2y^3}} \cdot 2(3y^2) - 1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {3y^2}{\sqrt{x^2+2y^3}} -1 \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (3,2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}(3,2) &= \dfrac {3}{\sqrt{3^2+2(2)^3}} = \dfrac{3}{5} \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}(3,2) &= \dfrac {3(2)^2}{\sqrt{3^2+2(2)^3}} -1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{12}{5} - 1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{7}{5} \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

\begin{align*} z - 3 &= (x-3)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(3,2) + (y-2)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(3,2) \\[5pt] z - 3 &= \dfrac{3}{5}(x-3) + \dfrac{7}{5}(y-2) \\[5pt] 5z -15 &= 3(x-3) + 7(y -2) \\[5pt] 5z -15 &= 3x - 9 + 7y -14 \\[5pt] -3x - 7y + 5z + 8 &=0 \\[5pt] 3x + 7y - 5z - 8 &=0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x^2yz + xy^2z + xyz^2$ at the point $(1,-1,1,-1).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

\[ w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(x^2yz + xy^2z + xyz^2 \right) = 2xyz+y^2z+yz^2\\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(x^2yz + xy^2z + xyz^2 \right) = x^2z+2xyz+xz^2 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(x^2yz + xy^2z + xyz^2 \right) = x^2y + xy^2 + 2xyz \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,-1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (1,-1,1) &= 2(1)(-1)(1)+ (-1)^2(1)+(-1)(1)^2 = -2 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (1,-1,1) &=(1)^2(1)+2(1)(-1)(1)+(1)(1)^2 = 0 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} (1,-1,1) &= (1)^2(-1) + (1)(-1)^2 + 2(1)(-1)(1) = -2 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

\begin{align*} w - (-1) &= (x-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,-1,1) + (y-(-1))\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,-1,1) + (z-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(1,-1,1) \\[5pt] w +1 &= -2(x-1) + 0 \cdot (y+1) - 2(z-1) \\[5pt] w +1 &= -2x - 2z + 4 \\[5pt] 2x + 2z + w -3 &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w = x^2 - y^2 + z^2$ at the point $(1,0,2,5).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as \[ w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^2 - y^2 + z^2 \right) = 2x \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( x^2 - y^2 + z^2 \right) = -2y \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( x^2 - y^2 + z^2 \right) = 2z \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,0,2)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (1,0,2) & = 2(1) = 2 \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} (1,0,2) & = -2(0) = 0\\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} (1,0,2) & = 2(2) = 4 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane: \begin{align*} w - 5 & = (x - 1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,0,2) + (y - 0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,0,2) + (z - 2)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(1,0,2) \\[5pt] w - 5 & = 2(x - 1) + 0y + 4(z - 2) \\[5pt] w - 5 & = 2x + 4z - 10\\[5pt] 2x + 4z - w - 5 & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sin (xyz)$ at the point $(1,1,\pi,0).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

\[ w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\sin (xyz) \right) = yz\cos(xyz) \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\sin (xyz) \right) = xz\cos(xyz) \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(\sin (xyz) \right) =xy\cos(xyz) \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,1,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (1,1,\pi) &= (1)(\pi)\cos(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi) = -\pi \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (1,1,\pi) &=(1)(\pi)\cos(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi) = -\pi \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} (1,1,\pi) &=(1)(1)\cos(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi) = -1 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

\begin{align*} w - 0 &= (x-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,1,\pi) + (y-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,1,\pi) + (z-\pi)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(1,1,\pi) \\[5pt] w &= -\pi(x-1) - \pi(y-1) - (z-\pi) \\[5pt] w &= -\pi x + \pi - \pi y + \pi - z + \pi \\[5pt] \pi x + \pi y + z + w -3\pi &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=e^x + e^y - e^z$ at the point $(1,1,1,e).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

\[ w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(e^x + e^y - e^z \right) = e^x \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(e^x + e^y - e^z \right) = e^y \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(e^x + e^y - e^z \right) =-e^z \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (1,1,1) &= e^1 = e \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (1,1,1) &= e^1 = e \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} (1,1,1) &= -e^1 = -e \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

\begin{align*} w - e &= (x-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,1,1) + (y-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,1,1) + (z-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(1,1,1) \\[5pt] w - e &= e(x-1) + e(y-1) - e(z-1) \\[5pt] w - e &= ex - e + ey - e - ez + e \\[5pt] -ex - ey + ez + w &= 0 \\[5pt] ex + ey - ez - w &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w = z\sqrt{y} - x$ at the point $(-1,4,1,3).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as \[ w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( z\sqrt{y} - x \right) = -1 \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( z\sqrt{y} - x \right) = \dfrac{z}{2\sqrt{y}} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( z\sqrt{y} - x \right) = \sqrt{y} \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (-1,4,1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (-1,4,1) & = -1 \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} (-1,4,1) & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{4}} = \dfrac{1}{4}\\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} (-1,4,1) & = \sqrt{4} = 2 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane: \begin{align*} w - 3 & = (x - (-1))\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(-1,4,1) + (y - 4)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(-1,4,1) + (z - 1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(-1,4,1) \\[5pt] w - 3 &= -(x+1) + \dfrac{1}{4}(y-4) + 2(z-1) \\[5pt] w - 3 & = -x + \dfrac{1}{4}y + 2z - 4 \\[5pt] x - \dfrac{1}{4}y - 2z + w + 1 & = 0\\[5pt] 4x - y - 8z + 4w + 4 & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: At which points on the surface $z = x^3 + xy$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as \[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), \] where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^3 + xy \right) = 3x^2 + y \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( x^3 + xy \right) = x \end{align*}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is \[ \left\langle 3x^2 + y, \, x, \, -1 \right\rangle. \]

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$ \[ \begin{cases} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} = 0 \\[3pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} = 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 3x^2 + y = 0 \\[3pt] x = 0 \end{cases} \]

From the second equation we get $x = 0.$ Substituting $x = 0$ into first equation, we obtain $y = 0.$

Finally, substituting $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ into our function, we get \[ z = 0^3 + 0(0) = 0. \]

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$

question.text: At which point on the surface $z= 3x^2 + y^2$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{v} = \left\langle 4, -2, -1 \right\rangle?$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as \[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), \] where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(3x^2 + y^2\right) = 6x \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(3x^2 + y^2\right) = 2y \end{align*}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is \[ \left\langle 6x, \, 2y, \, -1 \right\rangle. \]

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $\left\langle 4, -2, -1 \right\rangle .$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have \[ c \cdot \left \langle 6x, \, 2y, \, -1 \right \rangle = \langle 4, -2, -1 \rangle. \]

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system: \[ \begin{cases} 6cx = 4\\[3pt] 2cy = -2\\[3pt] -c = -1 \end{cases} \]

From the third equation, we get $c = 1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ 6(1)x = 4 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x = \dfrac{2}{3}. \]

And substituting $c = 1$ into the second equation, we have \[ 2(1)y = -2 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad y = -1. \]

Finally, substituting $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$ and $y = -1$ into our function, we get \begin{align*} z & = 3\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 + (-1)^2\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4}{3} + 1\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{7}{3}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf v$ at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}, -1, \dfrac{7}{3} \right).$

question.text: At which points on the surface $z= x^2+2x+y^2+2y$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf v\!=\! \langle -4, 0, 1 \rangle?$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

\[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), \]

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (x^2+2x+y^2+2y) \\[5pt] &= 2x+2 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (x^2+2x+y^2+2y) \\[5pt] &= 2y+2 \end{align*}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is

\[ \left\langle 2x+2, \: 2y+2, \: -1 \right\rangle \]

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $\langle -4, 0, 1 \rangle .$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

\[ c \cdot \left \langle 2x+2, \: 2y+2, \: -1 \right \rangle = \langle -4, 0, 1 \rangle. \]

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} c(2x+2) = -4\\ c(2y+2) = 0\\ -c = 1 \end{cases} \]

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\[ -(2x+2)=-4 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=1. \]

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have \[ -(2y+2) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y=-1. \]

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

\begin{align*} z &= (1)^2+2(1)+(-1)^2+2(-1) \\[3pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf v$ at $(1,-1,2).$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

\[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), \]

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(4x^2y+xy^3-6 \right) \\[5pt] &= 8xy+y^3 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(4x^2y+xy^3-6 \right) \\[5pt] &= 4x^2 +3xy^2 \end{align*}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is

\[ \left\langle 8xy+y^3, \: 4x^2 +3xy^2, \: -1 \right\rangle. \]

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} = 0 \\ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} = 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 8xy+y^3 = 0 \\ 4x^2 +3xy^2 = 0 \end{cases} \]

From the first equation, we get $y=0$ or $y^2+8x=0.$ So, we have two cases.

  • If $y = 0$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain \[ 4x^2 +3x(0)^2 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0. \]

  • If $y^2=-8x$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain \[ 4x^2 +3x(-8x)^2 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0. \] Substituting $x=0$ back into $y^2=-8x$ gives \[ y^2=-8(0) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y = 0. \]

So, in both cases, we have $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Finally, substituting these values into our function, we get

\[ z = 4(0)^2(0)+(0)(0)^3-6 = -6. \]

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,-6).$

question.text: At which points on the surface $z = \ln (1+x^2+y^2)$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

\[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), \]

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( \ln (1+x^2+y^2) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{1+x^2+y^2} \cdot 2x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {2x}{1+x^2+y^2} \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( \ln (1+x^2+y^2) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{1+x^2+y^2} \cdot 2y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {2y}{1+x^2+y^2} \end{align*}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is

\[ \left\langle \dfrac {2x} {1+x^2+y^2}, \: \dfrac {2y}{1+x^2+y^2}, \: -1 \right\rangle. \]

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} = 0 \\ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} = 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} \dfrac {2x} {1+x^2+y^2} = 0 \\ \dfrac {2y} {1+x^2+y^2} = 0 \end{cases} \]

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ while the second equation gives $y=0.$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

\[ z = \ln(1+0^2+0^2) = 0. \]

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$
